utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Good afternoon, ladies and gentlemen. Good afternoon to the interpreters and the technicians. Are you prepared? Are you ready for your very difficult task before you? For the record, shall we introduce the affair before the Chamber. First of all, Mr. Mark Dubuisson, would you please inform the Chamber of the case before it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This is case number IT-95-14/1-T, the Prosecutor versus Zlatko Aleksovski.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Dubuisson. I believe we are beginning with somewhat of a technical difficulty, because my colleague and I, Judge Vohrah and myself, have nothing on our screens, and this also applies to Mr. Mark Dubuisson. And the Defence and the Prosecution, does the Prosecution have something on its screen?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, the transcript does appear on the screens.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Well, you are lucky. You are very lucky. And the Defence? No? The Defence has nothing on its screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOKA
utterances.text: We have nothing either.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Well, in any case, we can continue while the technicians try to resolve the situation. So the second thing would be to allow for the Prosecution to introduce itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. I am Anura Meddegoda. Mr. Grant Niemann appears with me and Ms. Erasmus for the Prosecution. This afternoon, Your Honours, Mr. Niemann is on his feet before another Trial Chamber, and he may be here as soon as time permits, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: In any case, he will be here in spirit.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: He would certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours, I am Goran Mikulicic, and with Mr. Joka I appear for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Very well. We are noting now that we still have nothing on our screens. And my colleague Judge Nieto Navia is also lucky, because he has something on his screen. I see the problem has been overcome. Let us then continue. Mr. Mikulicic, I believe that we are continuing with Madam Cosic. So please bring Madam Cosic into the room.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, if you will allow me before we resume. I should like to raise another question which is related to one of the earlier days of the trial. You will remember that Dr. Bilandzic was called as a witness for Defence. Professor Bilandzic identified some maps, which were admitted as evidence, as D15 and D16. You will remember that on the back of these maps there was untranslated text. The Defence should like to state explicitly that this text and part of what appears on the back of these maps does not tender as evidence, nor does it consider it as a relevant document. We tender as evidence only the maps themselves on the front page of those sheets. I discussed it with my honourable colleague, Mr. Meddegoda, and I believe he concurs with this interpretation, but I should nevertheless like to hear him say so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: I am certainly thankful to Mr. Mikulicic, Your Honours, for the concession that he has made, and that he is not relying on the text on the back of those documents, D15 and D16, as part of the Defence case. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: I believe that we are all in agreement on this issue. Therefore, there is no problem. Would you please have the witness brought in, Mr. Mikulicic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Madam Cosic. Do you hear me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good afternoon. Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Would you please come closer to the microphone. There you are. Yesterday you took a solemn declaration to speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. Are you in the same position today, Madam?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Therefore, you will continue to respond to the questions put to you by Mr. Mikulicic. Thank you. Mr. Mikulicic, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mrs. Cosic.

utterances.speaker: ANKICA COSIC:
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Here we meet again in this Courtroom. Yesterday you answered a number of questions and stated various things. Today we shall have some more questions, not too long, and I should like to ask you to be so kind and answer them to the best of your recollection.

utterances.speaker: ANKICA COSIC:
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Cosic, yesterday you said that on one occasion you went on an official visit to the Kaonik facility to extend medical help to a patient; is that true?

utterances.speaker: ANKICA COSIC:
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Do you remember how long you were there?

utterances.speaker: ANKICA COSIC:
utterances.text: Only as long as it took to give the injection.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Well, how long would that be?

utterances.speaker: ANKICA COSIC:
utterances.text: Five minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: So all in all, you spent five minutes in Kaonik; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ANKICA COSIC:
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mrs. Cosic, yesterday you told us about the general impression left by the patients who came to the health centre in Busovaca from Kaonik. Could you tell us if, apart from patients from Kaonik, some other patients also came to the health centre? By this I mean civilians from the town, soldiers. Were there any such patients?

utterances.speaker: ANKICA COSIC:
utterances.text: Yes, there were.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Cosic, you don't have to bend towards the microphone. It is quite sensitive. Did you have an opportunity to offer medical help to HVO soldiers?

utterances.speaker: ANKICA COSIC:
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: What was their general state of health and what did they look like? Were they fit. I mean the HVO soldiers.

utterances.speaker: ANKICA COSIC:
utterances.text: Well, they were -- they looked -- there were among them some wounded, there were dead, others were dirty, tired, their hair uncut, unshaved. That's more or less what they looked like.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Did you notice, perhaps, some other ailments among HVO soldiers, perhaps some skin disease or something?

utterances.speaker: ANKICA COSIC:
utterances.text: Well, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Cosic, if I ask you now to compare the appearance of HVO soldiers and the appearance of Kaonik patients, what would you say? Who left a better impression on you, HVO soldiers or patients from Kaonik?

utterances.speaker: ANKICA COSIC:
utterances.text: Well, I think there was a difference. I mean, these did not look so bad as those who came like that, dirty. These were -- did not look like that, those who came. I did not have the impression that they were so dirty and unshaven. Perhaps somebody here and there, a little bit, but not too much. I did not notice that personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Cosic, let us clarify it for the record. When you say; "these were not too dirty and too unkempt that you did not notice it." Whom did you mean?

utterances.speaker: ANKICA COSIC:
utterances.text: I meant those who came from the prison.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mrs. Cosic, you said that in the waiting room of the health centre patients from Kaonik and other patients, civilian patients, or HVO soldiers, found themselves together in the waiting room at times. Did ever any incidents happen in -- on such occasions?

utterances.speaker: ANKICA COSIC:
utterances.text: Well, I could not tell you anything particular, as far as I can remember. I remember that we took note of that, that we took care to avoid it, because there were people wounded and discontent, with a grudge against the situation, and we took care of that. And we tried to remove them so as to avoid it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Cosic, when you say that people were not happy about the situation, discontent with the situation, who did they bear the grudge against? A particular -- I mean the Croat population.

utterances.speaker: ANKICA COSIC:
utterances.text: Well, I cannot really say. I cannot say exactly, you know, the situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Cosic, only a few questions more. If I remember it correctly, you said that you lived in the Village of Skradno, you used to live there in the village?

utterances.speaker: ANKICA COSIC:
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: How long have you been living in the village of Skradno?

utterances.speaker: ANKICA COSIC:
utterances.text: Eighteen years.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Do you perhaps remember if during the conflict there was any fighting in the Village of Skradno?

utterances.speaker: ANKICA COSIC:
utterances.text: No. No. In the village itself there was no fighting.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Did you hear that, perhaps, fire was exchanged somewhere outside of the village, around the hills?

utterances.speaker: ANKICA COSIC:
utterances.text: Oh, yes, yes. Yes. But I could not say where it was, because it came from outside, from above, from a certain height. And I could not, because I had -- I was under labour obligations and I could not really determine the situation. But one could hear the fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I see. Mrs. Cosic, I will show you now an air photograph, and I will -- and I shall ask you to comment upon it. Meanwhile, I have to ask Mr. Usher to --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This will be document D20.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Cosic, will you please look carefully at this photograph and tell us if you can recognise the aerial photograph from the air?

utterances.speaker: ANKICA COSIC:
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Cosic, if I told you now that this was part of the Municipality of Busovaca, which also includes your village, could you look at your village on this photograph. Take a good look.

utterances.speaker: ANKICA COSIC:
utterances.text: No. No. I really can't see my way around.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We do not need this photograph any more. Your Lordships, we have no more questions for the witness for the Defence, Mrs. Cosic. We have no more questions. Sorry, we should only like to tender this document, this air photograph, as evidence, as D20.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: No objection, Mr. Meddegoda?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: I have no objection, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Very well. Madam Cosic, you have just answered questions put to you by Mr. Mikulicic, and now you will answer questions put to you by Mr. Meddegoda, who may put to you -- is that true, Mr. Meddegoda, do you have any questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: A few questions, Your Honours. May I proceed, Your Honours?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Mrs. Cosic -- good afternoon, Mrs. Cosic.

utterances.speaker: ANKICA COSIC:
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: I will put to you a few questions on behalf of the Prosecution. You testified a while ago and said that when you went to Kaonik Prison, on the one and only occasion, you spent about five minutes in the prison premises; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ANKICA COSIC:
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: And do you remember when you went to the Kaonik Prison, the day on which you went to the prison?

utterances.speaker: ANKICA COSIC:
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Do you have at least a recollection of the month in which you went to the prison?

utterances.speaker: ANKICA COSIC:
utterances.text: It was a long time ago. All I can say is that it could have been in February or perhaps March. It was rather cold.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: And it was, as you testified yesterday, it was in the night that you made this visit?

utterances.speaker: ANKICA COSIC:
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: You also testified yesterday that the purpose of the visit, and you also testified this morning, this afternoon, that the purpose of the visit was to administer the injection to a detainee at Kaonik Prison?

utterances.speaker: ANKICA COSIC:
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Now, could you please tell me the circumstances which necessitated you to go to the prison? How did you happen to go to the prison?

utterances.speaker: ANKICA COSIC:
utterances.text: Prior to that, Zlatko came with that one man from the prison, and the doctor examined him and they consulted each other. The doctor said his opinion, and I, or perhaps my colleague, I cannot remember, filed that -- I cannot remember exactly, because we alternated, but the doctor said, in my presence, he told Zlatko that, if necessary, he could call and that he would send a nurse to administer the appropriate therapy.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: And what time was it when Zlatko -- when Mr. Aleksovski came to the health centre?

utterances.speaker: ANKICA COSIC:
utterances.text: They talked over the telephone.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Are you now saying that Mr. Aleksovski did not come to the health centre but spoke over the telephone?

utterances.speaker: ANKICA COSIC:
utterances.text: Oh, no. The first time, the first time they agreed that, if need be, the doctor would again send a nurse, and then they spoke on the phone, that he was bad, and that the therapy prescribed by the doctor should continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: What time was it when Mr. Aleksovski first came to the health centre that day?

utterances.speaker: ANKICA COSIC:
utterances.text: In the afternoon. I do not know the exact hour, but in the afternoon always.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Do you remember who examined the patient who was brought by Mr. Aleksovski?

utterances.speaker: ANKICA COSIC:
utterances.text: Dr. Stipac, Zvonmir Stipac.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: And was there a record made of such observation, of the fact that Dr. Zvonmir Stipac examined that patient?

utterances.speaker: ANKICA COSIC:
utterances.text: Were put down on paper, all that came. We filled forms and everything, as we always do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Were you present when the Dr. Stipac examined the patient?

utterances.speaker: ANKICA COSIC:
utterances.text: Not in the presence of examination. I filed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: But you were not present at the time of examination. You only filed the -- whatever note was made by Dr. Stipac?

utterances.speaker: ANKICA COSIC:
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: So you did not know what transpired between Dr. Stipac and the patient who was brought from Kaonik?

utterances.speaker: ANKICA COSIC:
utterances.text: Why no.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Sorry, I do not think the -- thank you. And how long thereafter did you get the telephone call from the accused?

utterances.speaker: ANKICA COSIC:
utterances.text: I could not give you the exact time, but as far as I can remember, not long -- not much later. Perhaps an hour or two.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: An hour, a few minutes?

utterances.speaker: ANKICA COSIC:
utterances.text: No, not minutes. Not minutes. One hour, perhaps two. It was a long time ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: And whom did Mr. Aleksovski speak over the telephone?

utterances.speaker: ANKICA COSIC:
utterances.text: One of the medical workers. I don't know who answered the telephone, but this was then conveyed to the doctor. That is the kind of co-operation with us. I cannot really know who answered the telephone.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: If you did not know who answered the telephone, how is it that you happened to go to the Kaonik prison that evening?

utterances.speaker: ANKICA COSIC:
utterances.text: But the doctor told me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Which doctor?

utterances.speaker: ANKICA COSIC:
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Who is the doctor who told you that?

utterances.speaker: ANKICA COSIC:
utterances.text: Dr. Zvonmir Stipac.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: And did you know who the patient was you were going to see?

utterances.speaker: ANKICA COSIC:
utterances.text: No. Not the name.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: And where in the Kaonik prison did you examine this patient?

utterances.speaker: ANKICA COSIC:
utterances.text: I did not examine him, I only administered the injection.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Where in Kaonik prison did you administer the injection to the patient?

utterances.speaker: ANKICA COSIC:
utterances.text: Excuse me?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Where in Kaonik prison did you administer the injection to this patient?

utterances.speaker: ANKICA COSIC:
utterances.text: In the prison, in a room. That room is -- there was a passage, it was night-time, I do not remember properly. I did not stay long. To the left there was a room. There were guards and that man whom I had seen before in the health centre, that same man.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: So you did not know the name of the patient to whom you went to administer the injection?

utterances.speaker: ANKICA COSIC:
utterances.text: Now I do not remember that name. And that doctor wrote out a prescription and on the basis of the prescription, I wrote it down and asked his name, but...

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Do you know whether such prescription is available in the health centre records now?

utterances.speaker: ANKICA COSIC:
utterances.text: I think so, yes, but I don't remember the name.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: And that was the only occasion on which you were sent to Kaonik camp?

utterances.speaker: ANKICA COSIC:
utterances.text: Yes

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Witness, you testified yesterday about an incident in Kacuni in January of 1993?

utterances.speaker: ANKICA COSIC:
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: And you said that in that incident, a person by the name of Ivica Petrovic got killed?

utterances.speaker: ANKICA COSIC:
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Did you know Ivica Petrovic?

utterances.speaker: ANKICA COSIC:
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: How did you know him?

utterances.speaker: ANKICA COSIC:
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: How did you know him?

utterances.speaker: ANKICA COSIC:
utterances.text: I think that he was born in the same village as my mother.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: And do you know what the city was?

utterances.speaker: ANKICA COSIC:
utterances.text: I think he was a Croat, but I didn't know his people.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: He was also a police officer at the time?

utterances.speaker: ANKICA COSIC:
utterances.text: I don't know that. Before, before the conflict, I knew of Ivica. As for his obligations, I didn't know anything about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Witness, you also said that in the health centre, you and your colleagues treated persons from all ethnic background, Croats, Serbs and Bosniaks without any kind of discrimination or differentiation, is that right?

utterances.speaker: ANKICA COSIC:
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Do you know whether -- the ethnicities of the persons who were brought from Kaonik camp were to be treated at the Busovaca Health Centre?

utterances.speaker: ANKICA COSIC:
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Did you know any of them personally, persons who were brought from the camp?

utterances.speaker: ANKICA COSIC:
utterances.text: Only by sight. I didn't know their names.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: And were there people from your village who were brought, or from the neighbouring villages, whom you knew by sight?

utterances.speaker: ANKICA COSIC:
utterances.text: While I was working, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Do you know whether there were any Serbs detained in the Kaonik camp?

utterances.speaker: ANKICA COSIC:
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Do you know whether there were any Croats detained in the Kaonik camp?

utterances.speaker: ANKICA COSIC:
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: And do you know whether there were all exclusively Bosniaks who were detained in the Kaonik camp?

utterances.speaker: ANKICA COSIC:
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Witness, also yesterday in the course of your testimony, you said that most detainees from Kaonik who were brought to the health centre complained mostly of stomach disorders as a rule.

utterances.speaker: ANKICA COSIC:
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Do you know whether detainees with injuries like contusions or abrasions or bruises or even lacerations were brought to the health centre for treatment from the Kaonik camp?

utterances.speaker: ANKICA COSIC:
utterances.text: No, no, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: You do not know that or you say that there were such prisoners were not brought to the camp?

utterances.speaker: ANKICA COSIC:
utterances.text: No, I mean I don't know that personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: And when prisoners were brought from Kaonik camp to the health centre, you said that they were first brought to the waiting room.

utterances.speaker: ANKICA COSIC:
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: And you also said that Mr. Zlatko Aleksovski would then come into the examination room and talk to a doctor or to a nurse saying that he had brought a detainee?

utterances.speaker: ANKICA COSIC:
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Were there occasions on which Mr. Aleksovski spoke to you personally when he brought a detainee from the camp?

utterances.speaker: ANKICA COSIC:
utterances.text: Well, we would only greet each other, that was all.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Yes, my question is were there occasions on which Mr. Aleksovski spoke to you personally when he brought prisoners from the camp?

utterances.speaker: ANKICA COSIC:
utterances.text: It was not necessary. He would simply bring in someone. If the intervention was needed, he would wait for the examination to be completed by the doctor. Sometimes I would tell him to wait, to Zlatko, and to the person whom he had brought in. Sometimes, if the doctor was available immediately, he would first talk to the doctor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: And do you remember Zlatko talking to the doctor, an instance in which Zlatko Aleksovski spoke to the doctor?

utterances.speaker: ANKICA COSIC:
utterances.text: I do not remember any specific situation, incident.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: I am asking you whether you remember Zlatko Aleksovski speaking to the doctor upon bringing a patient to the health centre.

utterances.speaker: ANKICA COSIC:
utterances.text: It is not quite clear to me, I don't understand which time period you have in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: I'll clarify my question. Do you remember seeing Zlatko Aleksovski talking to a doctor whenever he brought a patient or a prisoner from the Kaonik camp?

utterances.speaker: ANKICA COSIC:
utterances.text: Well, yes, I would fill in the form or perhaps I would be working in the adjacent room, the doors would be open. I was perhaps administering some therapy or doing some other kind of work and Zlatko would be speaking to the doctor. He would usually tell him that he had brought in someone and that that person was supposed to be examined and that was all.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Would he not say what the person was suffering from or complaining of?

utterances.speaker: ANKICA COSIC:
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: So Zlatko Aleksovski would say what the person was complaining of or suffering from?

utterances.speaker: ANKICA COSIC:
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: And what else would he say to the doctor?

utterances.speaker: ANKICA COSIC:
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: And were such observations, was the medical history so given to the doctor, was it recorded in any of the hospital records?

utterances.speaker: ANKICA COSIC:
utterances.text: Yes, a record was made. We kept records and we still do. Each name of the person brought in would be put down on paper, including therapy that was administered and the code for the diagnosis. There may have been cases where we didn't do everything, but it was customary to put everything on paper.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Did you personally maintain such records or make such notes of what Mr. Aleksovski said to the doctor or to the nurses?

utterances.speaker: ANKICA COSIC:
utterances.text: Only the name and the surname of the patient would be put down and the therapy that was recommended. Me and my colleagues, sometimes Zlatko, but we did the same with everybody else.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Yes, I understand that, Mrs. Cosic. But the history that was given to the doctor or to you or to the nurses, to the other nurses, was not recorded on the medical record?

utterances.speaker: ANKICA COSIC:
utterances.text: Well, we didn't use medical cards at that time because the services that were rendered were emergencies, so we would simply have forms where we would put down the code of the ailment, therapy that was administered and the name and the surname of the patient at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: So even on the medical form you would not record that?

utterances.speaker: ANKICA COSIC:
utterances.text: Medical form, we didn't have any medical forms at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: But you said a while ago there was a medical form on which you recorded the name and the therapy that was administered and record of the ailment, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: ANKICA COSIC:
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: And on that medical form, did you not record what was said by Mr. Aleksovski about the patient, what the patient was suffering from or what he was complaining of?

utterances.speaker: ANKICA COSIC:
utterances.text: No, only the code.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Did you consider it important to write it down on a medical form, the patient's medical history?

utterances.speaker: ANKICA COSIC:
utterances.text: Well, it's the doctor who does that. I would simply fill in the necessary information.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: As far as you are aware, was it done by a doctor whenever Mr. Aleksovski narrated the medical history or the causes of complaint?

utterances.speaker: ANKICA COSIC:
utterances.text: The doctor probably thought that it was necessary to put down the code only because the code would indicate the illness in question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Now, Mrs. Cosic, did you speak with any of the detainees whom you treated in the Busovaca Health Centre?

utterances.speaker: ANKICA COSIC:
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: You did not consider it important to talk to the patients, to find out what their problems were?

utterances.speaker: ANKICA COSIC:
utterances.text: The doctor would conduct the examination and I would -- I was in charge of administering the appropriate therapy.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: In the absence of the doctor, have you administered medication to any of the detainees who were brought from the camp?

utterances.speaker: ANKICA COSIC:
utterances.text: In the absence of the doctor, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: I have no further questions, Your Honour, in cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulcic, do you have any additional questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, just one question for purpose of clarification.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULCIC
utterances.text: Ms. Cosic, my learned colleague from the Prosecution asked you how it was that the doctor knew what the health condition of the patient was and what he complained of and you told him that Mr. Aleksovski would tell the doctor what the patient was suffering from, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ANKICA COSIC:
utterances.text: Mr. Aleksovski would only say that he had brought the patient and then the doctor would usher the patient in the surgery. He would examine the patient. And on the basis of the examination, he would give his diagnosis. And Zlatko Aleksovski would simply announce that the patient was complaining of such and such a disorder.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULCIC
utterances.text: I have understood that, thank you. Just one question, Mrs. Cosic. The patient who was brought in, was it possible for him to state his opinion on what he was suffering from?

utterances.speaker: ANKICA COSIC:
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULCIC
utterances.text: Did you see or hear that personally, did you see detainees from Kaonik say that in front of the doctor?

utterances.speaker: ANKICA COSIC:
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you, no further questions from the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Madam Cosic, I have a question for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Is it true or not that you also attended to HVO soldiers as well as detainees from Kaonik?

utterances.speaker: ANKICA COSIC:
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: It is true, okay. True or false, did Mr. Aleksovski accompany at times some of the patients and that once he appeared in civilian clothing and other times in military clothing, is that true or false?

utterances.speaker: ANKICA COSIC:
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Therefore, it is true that Mr. Aleksovski would often wear military clothing?

utterances.speaker: ANKICA COSIC:
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Therefore, you could identify the soldiers of the HVO because they were wearing military clothing, is that true or not?

utterances.speaker: ANKICA COSIC:
utterances.text: No, not because of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: How were you able to identify the HVO soldiers? How did you know they were soldiers?

utterances.speaker: ANKICA COSIC:
utterances.text: Well, we didn't exactly knew that they were soldiers. For them, they were all patients.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Yes, fine. But soldiers or some soldiers wore military uniforms, did they not?

utterances.speaker: ANKICA COSIC:
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Therefore my question is as follows: On those occasions when Mr. Aleksovski would wear military uniforms, what was the appearance of these military uniforms in relation to those uniforms worn by HVO soldiers? Were they similar? Were they the same? How would you answer that question? Do you understand the question?

utterances.speaker: ANKICA COSIC:
utterances.text: I think I do understand your question, I'll try to answer your question. Sometimes he would wear a camouflage uniform, but that uniform was not different from other uniforms that much. I mean this is not something that I was able to observe at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: I see. Then your answer suggests that the military clothing worn by Mr. Aleksovski were the same as those worn by HVO soldiers, am I correct in my summary or not?

utterances.speaker: ANKICA COSIC:
utterances.text: I didn't notice whether it was the same or different. All I knew was that Aleksovski had a camouflage uniform and sometimes he would also wear civilian clothes. As for the HVO soldiers, I couldn't know that they were HVO soldiers because at that time they were dressed in what they could find. I couldn't notice that and as for Zlatko, I knew what kind of uniform he was wearing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Very well, Madam Cosic, you have just completed your testimony here before the International Criminal Tribunal. The Chamber thanks you for appearing before it and we wish you a pleasant return trip to your country. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulcic, shall we continue?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, thank you. The Defence would like to call witness Zorka Ivancevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Good afternoon, do you hear me? You will now read the solemn declaration which the court usher has presented to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: You may be seated, madam.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Are you comfortable, Madam?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. THE COURT: You will now respond to questions put to you by Mr. Mikulicic, who is seated there. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mrs. Ivancevic. I am defending Mr. Aleksovski in these proceedings, and I have some questions for you. And I should like to ask you to answer them to the best of your recollection. Will you please tell us, for the record, the date of your birth and the place of your birth?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA IVANCEVIC
utterances.text: I was born on the 23rd of February, 1959, in Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Ivancevic, what is your ethnic origin?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA IVANCEVIC
utterances.text: I am Croat by origin.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Are you a practising believer?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA IVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Who is your faith?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA IVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Roman Catholic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Have you been living in Busovaca since your birth?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA IVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You still live there?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA IVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Ivancevic, could you tell us something about your education?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA IVANCEVIC
utterances.text: I have come from the secondary, from the high medical school in Zenica. I was general stream.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Do you remember, perhaps, when it was you came out of school?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA IVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. It was June 1978.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And did you get a job immediately after that?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA IVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Well, not immediately, but I did in 1980.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And where is it -- where was it?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA IVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In the health centre in Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And in the meantime, between 1980 to this day, have you held some other job or have you been on the staff of the Busovaca Health Centre all the time?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA IVANCEVIC
utterances.text: All the time on the staff of the Busovaca Health Centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And what were your duties in the health centre in Busovaca? Were they the same or different?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA IVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Different.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Could you perhaps list them?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA IVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I can. I was in the occupational medicine department, health care, emergency -- perhaps something else, but I cannot remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Do you remember, Mrs. Ivancevic, what was the ethnic composition of the staff in the health centre in Busovaca? What ethnicities did the personnel belong to in the former half of 1993, before the conflict?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA IVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do remember it. At that time we had about 65 to 70 people on the staff. Of them, I think that half of them were of Muslim origin. Roughly about the same percentage were Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Were there some other ethnicities employed in the health centre at Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA IVANCEVIC
utterances.text: There were also a couple of Serb employees.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You said that there were about -- that the staff comprised some 65 to 70 people. So this was quite a large institution, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA IVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Well, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: What area did it cover, I mean in terms of the services?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA IVANCEVIC
utterances.text: The area of the Municipality of Busovaca. Do you mean the number of inhabitants, the population? Well, at that time there were about 18.000 people.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Tell us, do you remember if the health centre in Busovaca had a department providing hospital treatment, where people could be hospitalised?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA IVANCEVIC
utterances.text: No. No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: So, Mrs. Ivancevic, what did you do when a patient required hospitalisation? What hospital did you refer them to?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA IVANCEVIC
utterances.text: We sent the patients to the hospital at Nova Bila.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: What was that time period that you are referring your patients there?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA IVANCEVIC
utterances.text: I mean 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And before 1993?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA IVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Before 1993 we referred our patients to the regional hospital in Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Ivancevic, do you remember if prior to 1993, that is before the conflict broke out, if there was a hospital at Nova Bila before that?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA IVANCEVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us why you stopped referring patients to the regional hospital in Zenica in 1993?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA IVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Towards the end of January, 1993, the fighting began. This was called the Muslim-Croat conflict. And at that time the road to Zenica was blocked so that we could not send our patients to the hospital in Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Do you remember, perhaps, when was the last time that you referred a patient to the Zenica hospital? Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA IVANCEVIC
utterances.text: I don't remember. I cannot remember exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You mentioned the conflict which was in January '93. How was it, that is, what event triggered the beginning of the conflict? Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA IVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. On the 24th of January, '93, I was to be on duty at the emergency service as of 1900 hours, and on my way to work a colleague told me that two men had been killed in the locality called Kacuni. And indeed that afternoon, at 3.15, I heard a powerful detonation when I was still at home. And then when I got to my place of work I learned what had happened. So that was my impression. And then, on the 25th of January, '93, a genuine conflict began.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Do you remember who were those individuals who were killed in Kacuni?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA IVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Do you know their names?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA IVANCEVIC
utterances.text: I know the name of one of them. That was Ivica Petrovic. And the other person was an unknown body. To us all the while it was an unknown person.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Where did you know Ivica Petrovic from, since you said you knew his name?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA IVANCEVIC
utterances.text: I knew Ivica Petrovic, I knew him personally, because he lived in Busovaca, so I knew him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You said you lived in Busovaca. How far from the health centre?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA IVANCEVIC
utterances.text: About three kilometres, more or less.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And at that time, while the fighting went on in Busovaca, how did you go to there? Was it safe?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA IVANCEVIC
utterances.text: No, it was hazardous. At times I walked, I went on foot, and, well, you know, depended on the situation. Sometimes by car and sometimes on foot, three kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: When the conflict began in the Municipality of Busovaca, you said it was towards the end of January, 1993, you said that the road was closed to Zenica. What about other roads? Were they passable? Could one take them to travel?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA IVANCEVIC
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, the Zenica road was blocked. That I am positive. But at that time, I think one could go to Travnik still.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: What about the supplies at the time? Did you have enough food, medical supplies? Could you please describe the situation, if you remember?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA IVANCEVIC
utterances.text: At that time there was food. We had enough water, electricity, we also had the heating. We had the heating as long as the coal stocks lasted. After that -- as a matter of fact, UNPROFOR made the heating possible. As for the medical supplies, well, you could say we had enough of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: When you say that UNPROFOR enabled, you mean the local UNPROFOR base?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA IVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Where was it accommodated, as against the health centre?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA IVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You mean how far was it? Well, about, perhaps, 800 to 1.000 metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Ivancevic, do you remember, in the -- just as the conflict broke out, so on the 24th, the 25th of January, '93, do you know what happened to the employed who were of Muslim origin in the health centre? Did you notice something that struck you, perhaps, as odd?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA IVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Not then. Later on, as the whole -- as it began to unfold, yes, it did seem odd that most of them, some who decided to then use their holidays, that is their holidays that were due them since 1992. Somehow it coincided in time with the outbreak of the conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Ivancevic, as an inhabitant of Busovaca, did you notice, perhaps, that as the conflict broke out the Muslim population began to leave Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA IVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I did notice that they were leaving to the nearest place, Kacuni, where there is a Muslim majority. It is some five or six kilometres from Busovaca. And I could really see that. It was noticeable. They left by passenger cars, those who had them, and those who lived in adjoining villages, they were also taking their livestock away, which was really odd. Don't you think so?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Did you wonder, then, did you ask yourself why were those people leaving?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA IVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't really remember how was it. It was strange and -- yes, I felt fear, but I did not really expect that anything else terrible would happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Ivancevic, tell us, how was the work organised in the health centre after the outbreak of the conflict? How did you operate?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA IVANCEVIC
utterances.text: I think that my impression was that we organised work quite well. We had enough of the paramedical personnel, so the nurses, we had two or three nurses even on a shift, on a 24 hour shift, and then we'll be free for 48 hours and, if need be, then we would return earlier, that is, we would not use all those 48 hours. So I think we did quite well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Did you have many patients when you were on duty?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA IVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, very many.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: How many, approximately? Do you remember?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA IVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Well, possibly up to 50 a day.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You say up to 50. What period of time do you have in mind? Could you be more specific? What month?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA IVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Well, yes, I can. It was in the beginning of the conflict, that is the end of January, early February. I think when they brought individuals from the Kaonik facility, that is when we were the busiest.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You mentioned the Kaonik facility and individuals brought from there. Did you ever visit the Kaonik facility?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA IVANCEVIC
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: But do you know what kind of facility was it? Do you know what it was before and what was it at the time of the conflict?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA IVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Why, yes. Before the conflict it was the barracks of the former JNA, and at the time of the conflict it was used -- its purpose was a facility, it was the place to protect people who were threatened. I know that. I never went there, but I know what it was before the war and what was its purpose during the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Do you know, Mrs. Ivancevic, that it was a military prison in Kaonik?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA IVANCEVIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't. I do not know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Did you personally, when on duty, come across patients who would be brought to the health centre from the Kaonik facility? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA IVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You mean the date?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: No, not the date. You could hardly remember the date. But if you do remember the date, very good. But I mean the period of time.

utterances.speaker: ZORKA IVANCEVIC
utterances.text: The end of January, early February. That was that period of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: As far as you can recollect, how many patients from Kaonik were brought to the health centre in Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA IVANCEVIC
utterances.text: I do not really remember how many, but I told you that we were very busy because of those individuals who were brought for medical examination. I think -- I don't know, I cannot exactly -- I cannot remember exactly, but some 30 or thereabouts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Ivancevic, were you personally ever in the proximity or did you have any contact with those patients from Kaonik?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA IVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us, if you remember, what complaints did these people have? What did they suffer from, what kind of medical help did they need?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA IVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. As a rule, they -- well, these were individuals, patients -- patients. When I say patients, I mean those individuals who were in the health centre. Usually -- I mean, I knew most of them, and they usually asked for the same kind of help that they came to the centre even before. That is, as a rule, high blood pressure or people who suffered from diabetes, or they came for the medication needed for that particular ailment and so. I mean, simply -- I don't know what to say. But, generally speaking, there were no major diseases. Same kind of illnesses that they suffered before. That is why they came

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Perhaps this would be an appropriate time for a break. After that you may continue. We'll take a 20-minute recess. --- Upon adjourning at 2.49 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Madam Ivancevic, we are going to continue. Perhaps it would be appropriate to tell you that behind you, you can see yourself, there are individuals, very nice people as you can see. You're doing a very good job for us all in ensuring that we can understand you. They're very nice, aren't they? So please try to imagine that when you're speaking with Mr. Mikulcic that there are these people who are acting on your behalf. So if you could make a pause between the question and the answer, it would be helpful for us so that we can understand you easily. Mr. Mikulcic, you now have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Ivancevic, let us continue where we stopped before the break. You mentioned that persons from Kaonik would also come as patients to your medical centre and you told us that they usually complained of health problems that they had before they were accommodated in Kaonik. Is it true that they suffered from some chronic diseases?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA IVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Ivancevic, who brought these individuals from Konjic to be examined at the health centre?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA IVANCEVIC
utterances.text: The detainees were brought to the health centre as patients by the guards and Mr. Zlatko Aleksovski.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Do you know Mr. Aleksovski from before the conflict or did you meet him at that time?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA IVANCEVIC
utterances.text: I met him at the health centre in late January, early February.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Do you think you would recognise him today?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA IVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I would.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us if you can see Mr. Aleksovski in the courtroom?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA IVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, he was the first person I saw when I entered the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Could you please point in his direction for the record. Can the record please reflect that the witness has pointed to the accused. Mrs. Ivancevic, the patients who were brought from Kaonik to be examined at the centre, were they tied up, did they have handcuffs?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA IVANCEVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Could you describe for us the procedure that was applied when they were received at the medical centre and what was the follow up of that procedure?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA IVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zlatko Aleksovski would usually call us at the health centre and he would usually announce that he had patients for us. These patients, once they are brought to the health centre, would go to the waiting room in the corridor where other patients would also wait to be examined by the doctor. There was one surgery. And patients would be examined by the doctor in that surgery. Only a doctor would be in that surgery and the patient, that is the detainee, would enter his surgery. The examination would take place there and then he would be brought back to the -- he would be brought to the nurse's office. So when they came to our office, they would have the prescription with the therapy that was recommended for that patient. My job as a nurse would be to make a record of his name, of the patient's name, to copy from the prescription form the therapy that was indicated. And after that administrative work was completed, depending on what was written on the prescription, if the patient had to receive an injection, I would then administer the injection. If the therapy involved certain tablets, the patient would have already received the tablets, the pills by the doctor. And I would make a note of that in another book. And that was the end of the examination of the patient at the health centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Ivancevic, do you remember if the patients had an opportunity to speak to the doctor themselves, to tell him what they were suffering from?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA IVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course. Most often they would be alone with the doctor and they were able to tell him about their problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Did you personally ever speak to one of the patients from Kaonik?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA IVANCEVIC
utterances.text: No, I did not, except for my part of the job. I mean, I was supposed to ask for his name and proceed with my part of the job.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Ivancevic, the procedure that you have just described, that is the examination of the patients from Kaonik, was the same procedure applied to all other patients at the health centre?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA IVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Did you have any different treatment for patients coming from Kaonik as opposed to other patients?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA IVANCEVIC
utterances.text: No, we did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Was there a case when the doctor or nurse refused to provide medical help to patients from Kaonik?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA IVANCEVIC
utterances.text: No, such things never occurred.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Ivancevic, you had the opportunity to see, personally, individuals coming from Kaonik?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA IVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Could you then tell us, could you describe for us how they looked? Could you compare the way they look with other patients that you normally received at the health centre?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA IVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can tell you about that. They were not different from other patients, but there was one thing that we could observe. The men, because they were only men, were unshaved. That is the only thing that we could observe. And it was something normal for such people because of the facility they were accommodated in. They were perhaps not as tidy as others.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Ivancevic, did you provide medical services to HVO soldiers at the medical centre?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA IVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, we did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: What did they look like in comparing with the patients from Kaonik?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA IVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Well, they were also untidy. You could see that they were very tired. That was all.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: How did you know that they were HVO soldiers?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA IVANCEVIC
utterances.text: They were wearing uniforms with HVO insignia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Would you recognise such insignia if you saw one?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA IVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I would.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: With the assistance of the usher, can the witness be shown Exhibit P-17. Could you please place the exhibit on the ELMO so that we can see it on the screen. Mrs. Ivancevic, you can see two types of insignia here, one that has been marked with No. 1, and the other marked with No. 2. Which of these two signs did you observe on the soldiers that received medical help at your medical centre in Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA IVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Well, the soldiers, or patients, rather. Yes, the patients to whom I gave medical help, I noticed that they were wearing the sign marked with No. 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: It's the HVO sign?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA IVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Did you ever see any of your patients wearing the insignia marked with No. 1, HV?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA IVANCEVIC
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Ivancevic, when Mr. Aleksovski came to the health centre, do you remember how he was dressed?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA IVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Sometimes he was wearing a uniform, but very often he was dressed in civilian clothes as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Do you remember when he was dressed in military uniform whether he was wearing any of these two insignia or maybe some other type of insignia?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA IVANCEVIC
utterances.text: That suit was without insignia. I didn't notice any insignia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Did he have any rank insignia, military rank?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA IVANCEVIC
utterances.text: No, I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you, we no longer need this exhibit. It can be removed from the ELMO. Mrs. Ivancevic, you mentioned that the procedure for the patients coming from Kaonik was the same as the procedure applied to all other patients at the health centre, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA IVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Does that mean you would sometimes have both members of the HVO and patients from Kaonik sitting in the waiting room?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA IVANCEVIC
utterances.text: I don't remember any such occasion, but it could happen, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Do you remember whether there was any incident in connection with that?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA IVANCEVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Did you notice what kind of relationship Mr. Aleksovski or the guard, what kind of relationship they had with the people that were brought from Kaonik?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA IVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Well, the relationship between Mr. Aleksovski and the guards with the patients, individuals from Kaonik, was very correct and humane.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Could you please be more specific. What exactly do you mean by that, "correct and humane"?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA IVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Well, they were not restrained in any way, they were treated as all other people who were waiting in the waiting room and I didn't observe anything special, anything different. I didn't see that they were treated differently as opposed to other patients who were in the waiting room. That was my impression.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Do you remember, Mrs. Ivancevic, at the time of the events, late January, beginning of February, how the work was organised at the health centre?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA IVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do remember. I already told you that we would work for 24 hours, at least we, the nurses. There were 15 or 16 of us. There were fewer physicians. When I came to work, when I would come to work, I would find my colleague, the physician actually, Dr. Bernardica Mioc, I am referring to the 24th and 25th of January. After that, I was on the same shift with Dr. Zvonmir Stipac, Dr. Srdjana Markovic, Dr. Nada Petrovic and Dr. Rozika Kordic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Ivancevic, what was the therapy that was most often prescribed to the patients from Kaonik?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA IVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Well, they usually received therapy for high pressure. And I remember one patient who was on insulin, who took injections for diabetes. Sometimes we would give injections for back pain. Here I am referring to patients suffering from chronic rheumatic diseases.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You've mentioned rheumatic pain and lumbar pain, what kind of therapy was administered to those patients? Was any are rest indicated or prescribed as therapy?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA IVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Well, it depended on how serious the case was. If the patient was in severe pain, Voltarin would usually be prescribed and the patient would have to be spared from work. And usually he was also referred home for treatment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: As such kind of therapy, and here I have in mind, rest, home treatment and so on, was such therapy prescribed to all the patients as well, not only individuals coming from Kaonik?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA IVANCEVIC
utterances.text: That therapy was prescribed to all patients who needed it. And even today, a doctor would indicate or prescribe for the patient to be spared from work if his condition requires so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Is it, therefore correct, Mrs. Ivancevic, that therapy, home treatment, rest and so on, is a common therapy today as it was before?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA IVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Did you ever notice while you contacted these patients, did you ever notice any bodily injuries, fractures or similar?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA IVANCEVIC
utterances.text: No, not during my shift.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Ivancevic, I think you've already told us that you've never been to Kaonik?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA IVANCEVIC
utterances.text: No, I have never been to Kaonik.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us and now I am asking you as an inhabitant of Busovaca. How did people dress at that time? Let me be more accurate. Was it common for inhabitants of Busovaca to wear parts of military and parts of civilian clothing, that is mixed things?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA IVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Why was that, what do you think?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA IVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I think there was a shortage of civilian clothes. So that people used it, that is, they would wear a civilian shirt and trousers and a military jacket to keep warm.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Do you perhaps remember shirts that people used to wear, did they, perhaps, have some patches with markings of an army flag or something on the sleeve? Do you remember?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA IVANCEVIC
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Ivancevic, you never went to Kaonik, but do you know if the medical personnel from the health centre went to Kaonik?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA IVANCEVIC
utterances.text: I did not go there, but I am positive that a colleague went from Kaonik for fumigation and that she was invited by Mr. Aleksovski.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Do you remember if any of patients from Kaonik showed any symptoms of skin disease or lice perhaps or some contagious disease?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA IVANCEVIC
utterances.text: I did not notice, nor did I hear it from my colleagues that there were any such diseases.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, we have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Mikulcic. Madam Ivancevic, you have just answered questions put to you by Mr. Mikulcic. Now you will respond to questions put to you by Mr. Meddegoda sitting there, if he has any questions for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Just a couple of questions, Your Honours, not very many.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mrs. Ivancevic. You have been living in Busovaca since your childhood?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA IVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: And you know, practically, you know most of the inhabitants of Busovaca, either by name or by sight?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA IVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, and my job also made me know all those people.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: And you, what would you say that the composition of Busovaca was prior to the conflict between the Croats and the Muslims?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA IVANCEVIC
utterances.text: I already told Mr. Goran, before the war in Busovaca, there were 18.000 people. I do not know exactly, but I think that it was about 50/50.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: And you have in the course of your work at the health centre, treated patients, detainees, who were brought from Kaonik camp to the health centre?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA IVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Could you repeat the question, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: In the course of your work in the health centre, as an employee, as a nurse in the health centre, you say you have treated detainees who were brought from the Kaonik camp?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA IVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, we did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: And do you remember about how many patients you may have treated from the Kaonik camp?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA IVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You mean per day?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Per day, about how many would you have treated per day?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA IVANCEVIC
utterances.text: I have already said about 30.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: About 30. And about how many would you have looked at, attended to, out of that 30 during your shift of work?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA IVANCEVIC
utterances.text: I already told how the work was organised in the health centre. All patients, say there are 30 of them, who would go into the examination room, into the surgery. The doctors also had to go into the room where the nurse was, to be filed in the book to be put on record. And then depending on what the prescription said, if it was a medication, they would be, they would be given it immediately with the doctor. Or, if it was therapy by injections, then we would do it in that room.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: So in the examination room, it would be a doctor and the detainee from Kaonik who would be in that room?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA IVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: And no one else would be present in that room during the time of examination, is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA IVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Could be, but not necessarily so. Could be, if that person said that he or she wanted to be alone with the doctor, that was permitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: If he did not want to be alone with the doctor, what would the procedure be?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA IVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Well, if he did not want that, then he could be escorted. I do not mean only official escort. I mean that two patients could enter the doctor's room at the same time, if they wanted to.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: So there would be more than one patient in the doctor's room at one -- at a given time?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA IVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: And would there be others as well, apart from the patients and the doctor, inside that room?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA IVANCEVIC
utterances.text: There was no need for it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Were there occasions on which Mr. Aleksovski would be present inside that room?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA IVANCEVIC
utterances.text: I do not know that. I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Is it that you don't remember, or is it that you do not know that?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA IVANCEVIC
utterances.text: I do not remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: And were there occasions on which the guards who escorted the detainees would be in the room with the doctor and the patient?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA IVANCEVIC
utterances.text: I have already said that they could be, but need not have been in.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Have you seen guards who accompanied the patient, the detainee, in the same room as the doctor and the patient?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA IVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Normally I do not enter the doctor's surgery. I had another room where I worked. And as for me, yes, guards would come together with the patient.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Thank you. Mrs. Ivancevic, you also said in the course of your testimony that the Kaonik -- I withdraw that question, Your Honours. Now, Mrs. Ivancevic, prior to the conflict, you said that the Kaonik facility was used as the former JNA barracks; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA IVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: And do you know what it was used as during the conflict?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA IVANCEVIC
utterances.text: During the conflict, I said it already, it was used to accommodate persons of Muslim origin, of Muslim ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Do you know people who were of Muslim ethnicity who were in the Kaonik facility, either by sight or by personally or by name?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA IVANCEVIC
utterances.text: I did know some of those individuals.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: And were there people from Busovaca who were detained in that facility?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA IVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Do you know whether, apart from the Bosniaks, Muslims who were there, do you know if there were any Serbs who were detained in that facility?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA IVANCEVIC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: And do you know whether there were any Croats detained in that facility?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA IVANCEVIC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: You also said, Mrs. Ivancevic, after the recess, that it was normal for people of -- normal for inhabitants in Busovaca to be dressed in military uniform, sometimes in military trousers and sometimes in military jackets and shirts.

utterances.speaker: ZORKA IVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I did say that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Did you on any occasion, were you dressed in military uniform and military trousers or in military jacket? Did any of your colleagues in the Busovaca Health Centre wear military uniform, trouser or military jacket during this time?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA IVANCEVIC
utterances.text: No, I did not, nor did my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Okay. You also said, Mrs. Ivancevic, that most of the witnesses (sic) who were brought from the Kaonik facility had complaints of high blood pressure and diabetes, and that they had no major diseases in that way?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA IVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Did you speak to any of those detainees personally?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA IVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Only as much as was needed, as much as I needed to, because of my job.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: And what conversations did you have with any of the detainees? Do you remember any conversation you had with any of the detainees whom you treated?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA IVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Who could remember after all those years? I really can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: But you do remember that some of them only had complaints of high blood pressure and diabetes?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA IVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: And do you know whether there were patients who were brought to Kaonik who suffered from bruises or contusions, abrasions or lacerations, of that sort, or an injury of that sort?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA IVANCEVIC
utterances.text: I did not see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: And do you also know that patients suffering from contusions and bruises and abrasions were brought to the Busovaca Health Centre from the Kaonik facility in the month of April and May of 1993?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA IVANCEVIC
utterances.text: I do not know about such individuals, and I said that I did not see them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: I have no further questions, Your Honours, on cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic, do you have any additional questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Your lordships, if I may, one question only.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Ivancevic, my learned friend from the Prosecution asked you if you or somebody else, that is another colleague of yours from the health centre, wore the military uniform, and you said they did not. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA IVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Tell me, what was your uniform and your colleague's uniform?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA IVANCEVIC
utterances.text: My uniform was the nurse's uniform, the same as it is today.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I have no more questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Madam Ivancevic, I have one question for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: You stated that you knew the people, neighbours, in Busovaca who were in Kaonik. Do you know why these persons were imprisoned?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA IVANCEVIC
utterances.text: I do not know that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: But you knew them?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA IVANCEVIC
utterances.text: I said I did, but I did not know why they were accommodated there. That was not part of my job. It wasn't up to me to question them about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Was there any type of criminal act that was carried out that explained why all these people were imprisoned in your town?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA IVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Again, I don't know. I wasn't interested in that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: I see. Well, Madam, Ivancevic, you have just completed your testimony here before the International Criminal Tribunal. We thank you for appearing and we wish you a pleasant return trip to your country. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic, now we have the benefit of Mr. Niemann joining us here in the courtroom. Shall we continue?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour, I wasn't available earlier. I was in another matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: No problem. We stated beforehand that you were here in spirit. Now you are also here in body. Mr. Mikulicic, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. I should like to say good afternoon to my learned friend, Mr. Niemann, and say that I am happy to see him here again. We should like to call our next witness, whose name is Ms. Zorka Ljubos.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Madam. Do you hear me? I realise that you speak French well.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do. No, a little.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Very well. You are now going to read the solemn declaration, which the court usher will hand to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Please be seated, Madam. I would like to inform you that behind you there are persons who ensure that we can understand you in your language. They carry on the interpretation.
