And so please take into account the fact that between yourself and Mr. Mikulicic, who is sitting there, who will be asking you questions, that there are all these individuals, and so I ask that you speak slowly, with pauses. Thank you. Is that possible for you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: You feel comfortable? Very well. Now, you will now respond to questions put to I by Mr. Mikulicic. Thank you. Mr. Mikulicic, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Good afternoon, Mrs. Ljubos.

utterances.speaker: ZORKA LJUBOS
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I am representing Mr. Zlatko Aleksovski in this case, and I should like to ask you some questions. So please answer them to the best of your recollection.

utterances.speaker: ZORKA LJUBOS
utterances.text: I understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Ljubos, would you tell us when and where were you born?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA LJUBOS
utterances.text: On the 5th of August, 1957, in Ravno, the Municipality of Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And what is your ethnic origin, Mrs. Ljubos?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA LJUBOS
utterances.text: I am a Croat.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Are you a practising believer?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA LJUBOS
utterances.text: Yes, a Roman Catholic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Ms. Ljubos, what about your education?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA LJUBOS
utterances.text: I completed the high medical school and the high school for social workers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: What stream of the medical school?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA LJUBOS
utterances.text: It was the general stream.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And when you completed the high medical school of the general stream, did you get a job immediately or did you continue with your education?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA LJUBOS
utterances.text: After the completion of my secondary education, I proceeded to study -- I enrolled in medicine, the study of medicine in Sarajevo, but I dropped out, and in 1977 I got a job as a nurse.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: So this was your first job?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA LJUBOS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Do you remember where that was?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA LJUBOS
utterances.text: I do. It was the health centre in Travnik, hospital in Travnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And how long were you there?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA LJUBOS
utterances.text: In the Travnik hospital I stayed about four months and a half.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And then?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA LJUBOS
utterances.text: And then I got a job with the health centre in Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Are you still with the health centre in Busovaca or not any longer?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA LJUBOS
utterances.text: Since 1994, that is September '94, I have been working in the Municipality of Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Which means that since -- between 1997 to '94 you were with the health centre in Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA LJUBOS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And what was your job?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA LJUBOS
utterances.text: In the health centre in Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: ZORKA LJUBOS
utterances.text: In the health centre in Busovaca I moved around all the departments that existed in peacetime.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And what was the staff of the health centre prior to 1993, prior to the conflict? Do you remember, roughly?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA LJUBOS
utterances.text: As regards the nurses, I think we were 17, I think, but I cannot be positive about it. And doctors. Doctors, before the war, there were some four or five, including also dentists.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Ms. Ljubos, what was roughly the ethnic composition of the staff of the health centre? Do you know?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA LJUBOS
utterances.text: Well, I couldn't give you the ratios, but it was a mixed ethnic composition. There were Croats and Muslims and Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: At the time when you were with the health centre in Busovaca, was it possible to hospitalise patients?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA LJUBOS
utterances.text: In the health centre at Busovaca there were no conditions for the hospitalisation of patients. We had no hospital beds. And the institution -- as an institution was not envisaged to provide hospitalisation by statute.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And do you know, if a patient needed to be hospitalised, what did you do then?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA LJUBOS
utterances.text: If the conditions, that is the illness, the ailment was such that a patient needed hospitalisation, then we frequently covered this need through homecare. We called that kind of treatment home treatment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Ms. Ljubos, you mentioned dentistry as one of the activities of the health centre of Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: ZORKA LJUBOS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us how long did the health centre extend this kind of medical care?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA LJUBOS
utterances.text: Under normal conditions, the dentistry was a regular aspect of the activity, until the bombing, that is the shelling, and that was 1992. That was in Travnik. But since the health centre was hit then and damaged, the dental surgery could not perform as before, so that the dentistry services were reduced, that is, we provided only the emergency dentistry treatment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: That is, there were no conditions because the building was damaged during shelling, and you could not extend the regular dentist services?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA LJUBOS
utterances.text: Quite, quite. That is the extractions or perhaps trephinations, for the prevention, or perhaps prophylactic measures and regular treatment that -- that was no longer done.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Could you please for us laymen explain what are the extractions and trephinations?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA LJUBOS
utterances.text: Well, it means the first aid. It means to open a tooth, and the first aid is simply to alleviate the pain. And tooth extraction means to extract, to pull out the tooth, that is, remove the tooth from the mouth.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I see. Ms. Ljubos, do you remember the beginning of the conflict in Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA LJUBOS
utterances.text: Yes, I do. It happened on the 25th of January, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: How is it that you remember that day?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA LJUBOS
utterances.text: Well, I remember that day because of the sound of sirens that we heard at that moment, which was something new for us at that time. I also remember that day because we started admitting some unusual patients, that is, people who had been wounded. And I also remember that day because of the fear that we all experienced.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Ljubos, are you aware of a facility called Kaonik?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA LJUBOS
utterances.text: I am aware of that name, Kaonik, but I've never been there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Ljubos, do you know what was the function of that facility before the break-out of the conflict in Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA LJUBOS
utterances.text: Yes. It was the barracks of the former JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And do you know what it was used for after the break-out of the conflict, that is, immediately prior to the outbreak of the conflict?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA LJUBOS
utterances.text: I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Ljubos, after the 25th of January, 1993, you said that there was an increase in the number of patients?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA LJUBOS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us more about the patients that you received at that time?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA LJUBOS
utterances.text: I can classify them as follows: These patients were brought to us from the Kaonik facility, and we also had members of the Croatian Defence Council, that is the soldiers. And, of course, the third group, the civilians who lived in the area for which the health centre was responsible.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: If I understand you correctly, that was the first time that you came across individuals that were brought there from Kaonik?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA LJUBOS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: When did that happen?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA LJUBOS
utterances.text: Since it was long time ago, I can only tell you that it was at the end of January, beginning of February, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Who brought these individuals, these patients from Kaonik? How did they get to the health centre?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA LJUBOS
utterances.text: These patients were brought in a vehicle under the escort of the warden of the facility, Mr. Zlatko. Sometimes they would also be escorted by one or two guards, depending on the number of patients that were brought in.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You've mentioned Mr. Zlatko. Do you know Mr. Zlatko Aleksovski?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA LJUBOS
utterances.text: Do you mean here in the courtroom?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Yes. Could you recognise him?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA LJUBOS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I could.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us where he is here in the courtroom?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA LJUBOS
utterances.text: He is behind you. He is sitting behind you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Can the record please reflect that the witness has pointed to the accused, who is sitting behind the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Ljubos, when did you first meet Mr. Zlatko Aleksovski?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA LJUBOS
utterances.text: As I already told you, I think it was in late January, early February, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Do you remember when Mr. Aleksovski would come to the health centre, how was he dressed?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA LJUBOS
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that. Very often he would be casually dressed. It was some kind of a mix of civilian clothes and camouflage trousers, for example. But he would also come in a camouflage suit, which, at that time, was normal type of clothes worn by men.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Ljubos, I will now show you a photograph with some military insignia. And I would kindly ask you to tell us whether you have seen, whether you saw such type of insignia on the clothes that were worn by Mr. Zlatko Aleksovski or, perhaps, some other individuals. Could the usher please place the exhibit number P17 on the ELMO. Did you see on Mr. Aleksovski, when he was dressed in military uniform, you said it was a camouflage uniform, or when he would wear only parts of camouflage uniform, did you see any of these patches?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA LJUBOS
utterances.text: No, I don't think I saw any of these patches worn by Mr. Zlatko.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Did you see any other kind of insignia?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA LJUBOS
utterances.text: No, I don't remember any insignia. I think he was casually dressed. I told you that he didn't wear any insignia or rank.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mrs. Ljubos, you've mentioned that while providing medical services at the health centre in Busovaca you also extended medical help to the HVO soldiers; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA LJUBOS
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us, or, rather, point to the patch. You see two patches on the screen, number one and two. Which one did you notice on the uniforms of the soldiers that received medical help at your centre?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA LJUBOS
utterances.text: Yes, it was a patch marked with number 2. This was the patch that was worn by HVO soldiers. But not all of them, because at that time they didn't have enough uniforms or suits.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Ljubos, as part of your job or as a resident of Busovaca, did you ever come across anyone wearing the patch marked with number 1?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA LJUBOS
utterances.text: No, never

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: We no longer need this exhibit, Mr. Usher. It can be given back to the registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: We spoke about patients that were brought either by Mr. Aleksovski or by some other guards from Kaonik to receive medical treatment at your centre. Could you tell us something more about their problems, their complaints?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA LJUBOS
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, these problems were connected with their prior ailments, problems with digestion, blood pressure, cardiac myopathy and similar ailments. Sometimes colds, for example.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: For the record, Mrs. Ljubos, for us laymen could you explain what these ailments are?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA LJUBOS
utterances.text: Stomach problems refer to problems with digestion. Cardiac myopathy is a heart condition.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: How would you describe these ailments? Are we talking about chronic diseases or acute diseases?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA LJUBOS
utterances.text: In most of the cases these were chronic diseases.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Do you remember, Ms. Ljubos, what kind of therapy was prescribed to these individuals?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA LJUBOS
utterances.text: The therapy usually depended on how serious the ailment was. Very often it was only parenteral therapy. Sometimes it would be also the therapy by injection.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Ljubos, for these type of ailments, the ailments that you came across at that time, was your impression that these ailments were more frequent during wartime, that the number of such patients increased?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA LJUBOS
utterances.text: I wouldn't say that the number of such patients increased. We were actually surprised to see, during that time, not a single epidemy, not a single infectious disease that was recorded at that time, which is an indicator of a relatively stable medical situation, health situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Do you mean that at the health centre you never recorded any infectious -- the existence of any infectious disease at the Kaonik facility?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA LJUBOS
utterances.text: Yes, you are right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Is it true, Mrs. Ljubos, that as part of your job you had direct contact with patients from Kaonik?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA LJUBOS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: What kind of impression did they leave on you? Did you think they were malnourished?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA LJUBOS
utterances.text: No, you couldn't talk about malnutrition. As for my general impression, they were, perhaps, unshaven, unkempt, but at that time it was not something uncommon. Most of the men looked like that. I didn't think that they were malnourished.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: The patients from Kaonik, according to what you can remember, did they leave an impression which was different from the impression left by other patients seeking help at the medical centre?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA LJUBOS
utterances.text: No. Bearing in mind the general circumstances, the prevailing conditions, my impression was the same in both cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Ljubos, did you ever notice or did you ever hear any patients from Kaonik complaining of some bodily injuries, like fractures, blows, bruises, abrasions, and so on?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA LJUBOS
utterances.text: Since we worked in shifts, 24 hour shifts, which were followed by 48 hours off duty, I really don't remember that while I was on duty. I don't remember ever seeing, ever noticing, anyone with such type of injuries.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Which physicians were on duty on your shift, do you remember?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA LJUBOS
utterances.text: Yes, I do. I was with Dr. Stipac, Dr. Mioc, Dr. Petrovic, Dr. Markovic and Dr. Rozica Kordic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Ljubos, do you remember how the patients from Kaonik were brought to the health centre?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA LJUBOS
utterances.text: Yes, I do. I think, that is I am sure, that they were brought in a vehicle or sometimes in a van.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You distinguish between the two, what do you mean by "vehicle"?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA LJUBOS
utterances.text: A passenger car. I don't remember the exact type, but it was a grey vehicle, grey metallic vehicle.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: At that time, did the medical centre dispose of an ambulance?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA LJUBOS
utterances.text: At that time, the medical centre had problems with ambulances. And as far as I can remember, we had only one at that time, only one that was in good condition.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: The patients who were brought to your centre from Kaonik, were they restrained in any way, were they handcuffed?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA LJUBOS
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: What was the procedure that was applied when they were treated?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA LJUBOS
utterances.text: The procedure was the same as for all other patients. If there were patients waiting in the waiting room, they would also have to wait. If the situation was urgent, then they would simply go to the doctor's surgery. After the examination and after the necessary therapy was prescribed, these patients would go to the nurse's office. And the nurse would then put everything on file, make a record of all the necessary information, including the therapy. And, if necessary, the nurse would also administer the therapy that was prescribed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: If the prescribed therapy involved some medication, how would you go about that? Where did you obtain medication and to whom was it given? I am referring to pills or tablets.

utterances.speaker: ZORKA LJUBOS
utterances.text: Well, the medication that was at the medical centre, that we had at the medical centre was given to everyone, everybody who needed such type of therapy.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Could you slow down a little bit, please.

utterances.speaker: ZORKA LJUBOS
utterances.text: Yes, I will. As I told you, the medication was administered to everyone who needed it, everyone who needed medical help, regardless of their nationality, gender or age.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Yes, I am clear about that, maybe you haven't understood my question, so I will rephrase it. How did the medical centre obtain medication?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA LJUBOS
utterances.text: The medication came from the reserves that we had. According to the regulations, all medical institutions, including medical centres such as ours, were required to have what we called NEP, it's an abbreviation that refers to reserves in case of war. So I think all these reserves were pulled out so that we could satisfy the needs of all the patients who needed such medication.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Does that mean that, Mrs. Ljubos, that when the physician would prescribe certain therapy that the patient would immediately receive that medication?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA LJUBOS
utterances.text: Well, if the therapy involved pills or tablets, then the patient would be immediately given these pills together with the instructions on how to use the medication. The first dose would usually be administered right there at the health centre and it was to be followed up according to the prescription, to the therapy indicated by the physician.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that the patients would come for check ups if that was indicated by the physician?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA LJUBOS
utterances.text: Yes, that would happen very often, depending on the type of disease. These patients had to come for check ups within, I don't know, five, seven or ten days depending on the case and the disease in question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Do you remember, Mrs. Ljubos, any case involving home treatment, any case where home treatment was prescribed for the patient by the physician?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA LJUBOS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I remember. This is the kind of procedure that we apply today. Very often the physician indicates home treatment as the necessary therapy. Home care, it's a perfectly normal situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Ljubos, as far as you can remember, were patients able or given opportunity to communicate with the physician alone "tete a tete?" I am referring to the patients coming from Kaonik.

utterances.speaker: ZORKA LJUBOS
utterances.text: Yes, of course. If several were brought in, then only one would enter the surgery first and complain to the physician and so on. I mean, it was normal procedure. They were able to have direct contact with the physician.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: During such examination, was the guard or Mr. Aleksovski present there at the surgery?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA LJUBOS
utterances.text: Well, it was not obligatory, sometimes they would remain if the waiting room and wait and they would be left without Mr. Aleksovski or without guards. But we also had cases of patients being there alone with the doctor without the presence of the guards or the warden.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Could you describe for us, in case you had opportunity to see that, what was the treatment or attitude towards the patients from Kaonik by Mr. Aleksovski or the guards who would bring such patients to the health centre?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA LJUBOS
utterances.text: I think I can describe it as a normal attitude, casual attitude. And here, I mean, I am referring to Mr. Aleksovski and other guards as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Ljubos, are you aware of any situation where the doctor or the nurse would refuse to examine or offer medical help to any of the patients from Kaonik?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA LJUBOS
utterances.text: I think I can say with pride that such a thing never happened and I am speaking on behalf of my colleagues as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You've mentioned a while ago, Mrs. Ljubos, that due to shortages of adequate clothing, it was customary for the residents of Busovaca to wear parts of military clothing, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA LJUBOS
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Did you personally or anyone else at the health centre have to wear parts of military clothing?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA LJUBOS
utterances.text: No, no. We wore our white coats.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: This concludes my examination, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: I believe this is a good time to take a break before we begin with cross-examination. So, therefore, we should have a fifteen minute recess now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Mr. Niemann or Mr. Meddegoda, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Mrs. Ljubos, there's a couple of matters I wanted to clear up if I may. From the transcript, it was a bit confusing as the time you were actually at the health centre. And, if I can, I would like to sort that out with you. Is it correct to say that you were employed at the health centre from 1987 to 1994, is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA LJUBOS
utterances.text: No, it is not. Since 1977 until 1994, that is September '94.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I see. And what happened after 1994, you left there, did you?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA LJUBOS
utterances.text: For personal reasons, I had some health problems, so I quit my job. Or, rather, I moved to another organisation, social workers, I also completed school for social workers.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I don't want the go into that, I just wanted to establish that you didn't stay there after 1994. I think you said you lived in the Town of Rodna in Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA LJUBOS
utterances.text: You didn't get me quite well, Ravan, R-a-v-a-n, Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And was Ravan town where the Croatian people living in and Muslims as well?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA LJUBOS
utterances.text: Yes, I was born in Ravan, but I live in the Town of Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I see. And during 1993 you were living in Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA LJUBOS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Okay. Now where you live in Busovaca, did you have any friends or neighbours who were Muslim people?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA LJUBOS
utterances.text: My colleagues, neighbours, people I saw daily, among them, there were also some Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And did any of those people go to the Kaonik camp that you can remember?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA LJUBOS
utterances.text: I don't think I could remember the individual names, but I saw people that I used to know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: No, I don't want you to name them, it's a long time ago. The people that went to the camp that you knew, they were people of good character in the community, were they?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA LJUBOS
utterances.text: In principle, my personal view says that all people are good, with some few exceptions.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I am not suggesting -- what I am saying to you is that, so far as you're concerned, they weren't criminals or behaved in an antisocial manner, they were just ordinary citizens, just like yourself?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA LJUBOS
utterances.text: Were you expecting an answer?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Do you agree with that, do you?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA LJUBOS
utterances.text: In principle, yes. It's not up to me to really judge anyone how good or how bad he is.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: But you would know whether someone was an notorious criminal or had a really bad record or something like that, and these people didn't fall into this category? That's the point I am really trying to raise.

utterances.speaker: ZORKA LJUBOS
utterances.text: I couldn't know if anyone had a police record or not. But, of course, one knew if somebody was a petty thief or something like that. Something that is common, of course, from daily contact.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Do you know why the people that you knew that ended up in Kaonik, why they went there?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA LJUBOS
utterances.text: I couldn't answer that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And what were the circumstances when you first met Mr. Aleksovski, can you remember when you first met him?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA LJUBOS
utterances.text: Since I didn't know the gentleman before, as I said, towards the end of January, beginning of February, 1993, I met Mr. Aleksovski in the health centre when he brought patients.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And did he actually have a conversation with you or did you just see him there and found out that that was his name?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA LJUBOS
utterances.text: Well, those were unofficial, off the record conversations by and large; good afternoon, good afternoon, how are you, how are you. I'd never had any particular contact with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: The prisoners that were brought in from Kaonik, did they -- what were they, what was their -- what were they like in their psychological presentation? Were they nervous or did they appear fearful or anything of that nature that you saw?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA LJUBOS
utterances.text: To be quite frank, we were all nervous at that time in view of the conditions, nothing particular. We were simply afraid of an uncertainty. We were all slightly fearful, so they were not different from the rest of people around.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: No further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulcic, do you have any additional questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Lordship, we have no additional questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Madam Ljubos, the Chamber has no questions to put to you, so this is the end of your testimony here at the International Tribunal. We would like to thank you for coming and wish you a pleasant return to your country. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulcic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, we have no more witnesses for today, so that we cannot call any other witness today. Tomorrow we shall continue adducing evidence, so will you please bear that in mind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Before we end this session, with your permission, in this spirit, and also discrete spirit of the activities of this Chamber, could we know whether or not it will be possible to finish with all of the witnesses tomorrow or not? I believe that our list mentions three witnesses and that will end the list of witnesses for this week. The question that I am asking is whether or not it will be possible to finish the list tomorrow or whether or not we will require to be here again Friday?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, the Defence would like to point out the fact that there are still two witnesses, Mrs. Kata Vidovic and Mr. Jelko Percinlic. We shall be calling them tomorrow. At the moment, I believe that Ms. Kata Vidovic will not take too much time. Mr. Percinlic will be a witness who may take some more time. But I think I believe that, yes, that we could finish tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Very well, if we finish tomorrow, very well, otherwise we will be here as well on Friday. In any case, let's make the best of the time we have available to us because the Chamber also has other work it has to do. Nonetheless, we will be here on Friday if necessary. If we can finish with this tomorrow, all the better. For the time being, we have completed today's work and we'll meet again tomorrow morning at nine o'clock. Thank you to you all. Tomorrow, see you tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: 4.55 p.m., to the reconvened on Thursday, the 18th day of June, 1998, at 9.00 a.m.
